title: Reading Frankenstein Through Its Frames
text:
Scholars have long read Mary Shelley's Frankenstein as more than a tale of a scientist's ambition. The novel is framed by letters, so the story reaches the reader through several narrators whose reliability is never fully settled. This layered structure invites the reader to question who is truly responsible for the creature's suffering. Many critics regard the frame as a deliberate device that distances the horror while intensifying its moral weight.

Other readers, however, emphasize the novel's engagement with the scientific debates of its own era, particularly the galvanism experiments that seemed to promise the reanimation of matter. On this account, Victor Frankenstein is less a villain than a man who mistakes knowledge for wisdom. The creature, who learns language by listening to a family through a crack in a wall, becomes the novel's most eloquent voice. The ambiguity between victim and monster is therefore central rather than incidental.

questions.text: What does the framing structure most likely suggest about the reader's judgments?
options: The reader should accept the narrators' accounts without question
The reader is invited to question who is truly responsible
The reader should ignore the moral dimension of the story
The reader will find the story easy to follow

questions.text: Why might the creature's portrayal be considered central rather than incidental to the novel?
options: Because the creature is the only character who speaks
Because it makes the boundary between victim and monster ambiguous
Because the scientist is shown to be entirely good
Because the story is set in a large city

paragraph_translations: Los estudiosos han leído durante mucho tiempo Frankenstein de Mary Shelley como algo más que una historia sobre la ambición de un científico. La novela se articula mediante cartas, de modo que el relato llega al lector a través de varios narradores cuya fiabilidad nunca queda del todo resuelta. Esta estructura en capas invita a preguntarse quién es realmente responsable del sufrimiento de la criatura. Muchos críticos consideran que el marco es un recurso deliberado que distancia el horror mientras intensifica su peso moral.

Otros lectores, en cambio, subrayan la relación de la novela con los debates científicos de su propia época, en particular los experimentos de galvanismo que parecían prometer la reanimación de la materia. Según esta lectura, Victor Frankenstein es menos un villano que un hombre que confunde el conocimiento con la sabiduría. La criatura, que aprende el lenguaje escuchando a una familia a través de una grieta en la pared, se convierte en la voz más elocuente de la novela. La ambigüedad entre víctima y monstruo es, por tanto, central y no accesoria.
